subject: Cloud Computing
title: Docker: Containers Change Everything
description: A micro-lesson that makes Docker: Containers Change Everything usable.

hook.text: In 2013, a startup showed technology that could package any application into a portable box.

buildup.text: Docker containers were lighter than virtual machines. They started in seconds, not minutes.

discovery.text: A container bundles your code and dependencies together. It runs the same everywhere.

twist.text: Docker delighted developers but created chaos — thousands of containers to track and manage.

climax.text: Docker didn't replace virtual machines. It created a new layer on top of them.

punchline.text: Containers are tiny, portable, and everywhere now.

quiz.question: How do Docker containers differ from virtual machines?
options: Containers are lighter and start in seconds instead of minutes
Containers require dedicated physical hardware to run
Containers can only run one application at a time globally

details.summary: Docker launched in 2013 and made containers accessible to developers by packaging applications with all their dependencies into portable, lightweight units. Containers start in seconds, use fewer resources than VMs, and run consistently across any environment.
details.whyItMatters: Docker transformed how software is packaged and deployed in the cloud. Containers solved the it-works-on-my-machine problem and enabled microservices architecture at scale.
takeaways: Docker made containers accessible to mainstream developers
Containers package apps with all dependencies for portability
They start in seconds and use fewer resources than VMs

faq.question: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
faq.answer: Virtual machines include a full operating system and run on a hypervisor. Containers share the host OS kernel and only package the application and its dependencies. This makes containers much lighter, starting in seconds versus minutes and using megabytes versus gigabytes.

faq.question: Why was Docker so impactful?
faq.answer: Container technology existed before Docker, but Docker provided a simple developer experience, a standard image format, and a public registry for sharing images. It made containerization practical for everyday development, not just specialized infrastructure teams.
